title: Queen against rook II: how to reach Philidor
summary: The ladder that walks the king to the edge, the second-rank defence and the diagonal position.
step.intro: Last lesson you won from the Philidor position. Today is the road to it. This is the second-rank defence: the black king is on the edge and the rook, on the rank next to it, cuts off our king. As long as it stays there our king cannot get in, and the rook also threatens checks on b7 and e6. Euwe published this position in 1958. It is a win, and there is one aim: bring our king in front of the black king and reach Philidor.
step.stale: First, what not to do. Here the queen went to d6, too close. The rook checked on b7, the king went to c6 and the rook offered itself on b6. If the king takes, the black king is stalemated. If the queen takes, the same. And if the king runs, the checks never end. A draw. The rule from last lesson still holds: queen far, king near.
step.open: The first two moves are learned by heart. A queen check along the diagonal, which sends the king to d8, and then a quiet king move, sideways and not forward.
step.open.hint: Qf5+ and, after Kd8, Kc5. On c6 the king would be checked by the rook from e6.
step.open.done: Look at the king on c5: the rook has no good check, and the black king has to choose a side.
step.fork3: From here Black has three defences. The king returns to c7. Or the king runs the other way, via e8. Or the rook leaves the king and goes far away to check from behind. Let us see the first two move by move. In both the pattern is the same: the queen checks to gain time, the king steps forward, and Philidor appears at the end.
step.a1: The black king returned to c7. Centralise the queen on d5. After the rook comes to d7, check on e5 and walk the king to b5.
step.a1.hint: Qd5, then Qe5+ and Kb5. The white king goes round along the b-file.
step.a1.done: The black king is already on the b-file, and our king is beside it. Now the queen has to be brought into place.
step.a2: Now the move that is hard to find: the queen goes to e8, behind everything, and takes squares from the black king. Then it returns to e4, the king enters on c6 and the queen closes in on d5 and d8.
step.a2.hint: Qe8, Qe4, Kc6, Qd5 and Qd8. At the end the black king is on a7 with the rook on b7, and our king on c6.
step.a2.done: Look at the position sideways: black king and rook on the edge, our king a knight's move away, queen on the file beside them. It is Philidor, on the a-file, with Black to move. The rook falls.
step.c1: Second defence: the black king runs via e8. Chase it with a check on c8 and bring the king to d6. When the rook goes to a7, a new check on c4 and the king advances to e6.
step.c1.hint: Qc8+, Kd6, Qc4+ and Ke6. A check to gain time, the king one step forward.
step.c1.done: The black king has been pushed to the other corner, and our king went with it, always in front.
step.c2: Finish it. Check on c5, queen to the centre on d5, and the king enters on f6 uncovering the queen's check. Then the triangle you already know: h1 and h5.
step.c2.hint: Qc5+, Qd5, Kf6+, Qh1+ and Qh5.
step.c2.done: Philidor again, now in the g8 corner. Two different defences, the same ending.
step.checks: The third defence is for the rook to run far away and give checks. The answer is a principle that holds for the whole endgame: before advancing the king, take the checking squares away from the rook. In this position from Nunn the black king and rook are on the second rank and our king wants f6, but the rook would check on g7 and g6 without end.
step.quiet: Instead of checking, prepare. The queen goes to d8 and then to d4, from where it watches g7. Only then does the king go in, and the rook's checks are over in two moves.
step.quiet.hint: Qd8 and, after Kh7, Qd4. To the rook checks the king answers f6 and f7.
step.quiet.done: The checks are over, and the rook is stuck next to its king. A quiet queen move is worth more than a check: Smerdon says the moves that make most progress in this endgame are hardly ever checks.
step.diagonal: One more position to remember: the diagonal. Black king, rook, our king and queen, all four on the same diagonal. The queen is ready to give a discovered check as soon as our king steps aside. But it is our move, and we need it to be Black's. You know the cure: a queen triangle.
step.discover: Pass the move with the queen: f4, check on f5 and back to e5. The rook will have to go to b7; then the king goes to c6 with discovered check, and the queen closes in on a1 and a5.
step.discover.hint: Qf4, Qf5+, Qe5. Then Kc6+, Qa1+ and Qa5.
step.discover.done: Philidor, with Black to move. The diagonal position is six moves away from it.
step.ladder: And when the black king is still far from the edge? This is where the ladder comes in. This position is from Walter Browne's rematch against the computer Belle, in 1978. The black king and rook are on the same file; our king is on the same rank as the black king, two files away. The recipe has three beats: check, check, and the king steps down one square. The position repeats one rank closer to the edge.
step.climb: Go down the ladder twice. Check on g7, check on h6, king to e4. And again: check on g6, check on h5, king to e3.
step.climb.hint: Qg7+, Qh6+, Ke4. Then Qg6+, Qh5+, Ke3. The queen checks from behind; the king only moves once the black king is back on the rook's file.
step.climb.done: The black king left the fifth rank and reached the third without being able to do anything. One more rung and it is on the edge, where the rook runs out of room: that is how Browne won the bet, on the last move allowed.
step.recap: Three ideas to take away. One: against the second rank, check on f5 and king sideways; then a check to gain time and the king one step forward, until Philidor. Two: before advancing the king, take the rook's checks away with a quiet queen move. Three: far from the edge, the ladder: check, check, king steps down. And the queen never hugs the cornered king.
step.finish: Your turn against the machine, from the second-rank defence. Start with the two moves you know by heart and see which defence it picks. If it lets the rook loose, take the checks away before advancing.
ex.e01: White to move. The second-rank defence. What is the first move?
ex.e01.hint: A queen check that does not come close to the king.
ex.e01.solution: Qf5+. The black king goes to d8 and the queen stays far away, giving no stalemate chances. Qd6 draws: the rook checks on b7 and then offers itself on b6.
ex.e02: White to move. The black king went to d8. Where does our king go?
ex.e02.hint: Forward it gets checked by the rook on the sixth rank. Try sideways.
ex.e02.solution: Kc5. On c6 the rook would check on e6 and set up another defence. On c5 the king cannot be checked, and Black has to decide.
ex.e03: White to move. The rook has just gone to b7. Which move gains time and reaches Philidor?
ex.e03.hint: The queen and the black king are on the same diagonal, and our king is in between.
ex.e03.solution: Kc6+. The king leaves the diagonal and the queen gives discovered check; the black king goes to the edge and the queen closes in on a1 and a5.
ex.e04: White to move. The ladder position. What is the first check?
ex.e04.hint: The queen checks on the black king's file, from behind.
ex.e04.solution: Qg7+. The black king goes to h4, the queen gives the second check on h6 and, when the king returns to the g-file, our king steps down.
ex.e05: White to move. The black king is near the corner with the rook beside it. Find a queen move that gives the rook no check.
ex.e05.hint: Beware of the check on c6: the black king goes to b8 and the rook sets up the stalemate on a6.
ex.e05.solution: Qe5 (or Qd4). The queen stays far away and controls the central squares; the rook has no useful check. After Qc6+ and Kb6 the rook checks on a6 and any capture is stalemate: Berger's trap, from 1889.
ex.e06: White to move. Our king wants f6, but the rook would give checks. Prepare the entry with two queen moves.
ex.e06.hint: First the back rank, then a central square from which the queen watches g7.
ex.e06.solution: Qd8 and, after Kh7, Qd4. Now the check on g7 is met by Kf6, and the checks soon run out.
ex.e07: White to move. If it were Black's move, the rook would have to retreat and the discovered check would follow. Pass the move.
ex.e07.hint: A queen triangle: leave the square, give a check and come back.
ex.e07.solution: Qe3, Qd3+ and Qd4. The same position with Black to move: the rook goes to b7 and the king enters on c6 with discovered check.
ex.e08: White to move. In the middle of the ladder: go down one more rung.
ex.e08.hint: A check on the king's file, a check on the next file, and only then the king.
ex.e08.solution: Qg6+, Qh5+ and Ke3. The black king and rook went down one rank and our king followed.
ex.e09: White to move. The end of the ladder: the black king is on the edge and the rook ran to the corner. Win the rook with three checks.
ex.e09.hint: The final square is g7: from there the long diagonal reaches a1.
ex.e09.solution: Qe4+, Qh7+ and Qg7+. The black king cannot get out of the way, and from g7 the queen checks and attacks the rook on a1. That is how Browne won the rematch against Belle.
ex.e10: White to move. Second rank, with the black king on the b-file. Find the quiet queen move and bring the king to c6.
ex.e10.hint: The queen goes to the back rank, behind the black king, and then returns to the e-file with another quiet move.
ex.e10.solution: Qe8, Qe4 and, after the rook check, Kc6. From e8 the queen takes b8 and c8 from the black king; from e4 it watches b7 and prepares the king's entry. From there the queen closes in on d5 and d8: Philidor.
ex.e11: White to move. The black king ran to the kingside. Chase it with checks and advance the king until the queen reaches d5.
ex.e11.hint: Check on c4, king to e6, check on c5, and then the queen in the centre.
ex.e11.solution: Qc4+, Ke6, Qc5+ and Qd5. Each check gains a tempo for the king to advance. With the queen on d5 and the king on e6, the next move is Kf6 with discovered check, and Philidor appears in the corner.
key.second: The second-rank defence, by Euwe (1958), as shown on Wikipedia. It is won with Qf5+ and Kc5.
key.diagonal: The diagonal position, from Unto's Lichess study: queen triangle, discovered check and Philidor.
key.ladder: The ladder, from Browne's rematch against Belle (1978): check, check, king steps down one square.
key.berger: Berger's trap (1889), quoted by Wikipedia: the check on c6 followed by Kb6 lets the rook offer itself on a6, and it is a draw.
history: Max Euwe published in 1958 the analysis of the second-rank defence used in this lesson, and Berger, in 1889, was already showing the stalemate trap near the corner. But it was a computer that showed the world how hard this endgame is. In December 1978 Ken Thompson's Belle defended the rook against grandmaster Walter Browne with a database that knew the best move in every position. Browne did not win in fifty moves. In the rematch, on 30 December, he took the black king to the edge with a ladder of checks, two checks and one king step at a time, and captured the rook on exactly the fiftieth move. The authors of the report written at the time say that players got stuck with about fifteen moves to go, not knowing how to cross the rook's barrier. That barrier is the subject of the next lesson.
practice: The second-rank defence, against the clock or without it. You know the first two moves by heart; from there, a check to gain time, the king one step forward, and Philidor.
